newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech banks lick their wounds after crown crisis.
newsitem.headline: Czech banks lick their wounds after crown crisis.

text.p: The Czech banking sector will be hit by falling profits and the threat of bankruptcies or mergers of small banks as a consequence of recent central bank interest rate hikes to defend the Czech crown, analysts say.
The extent of the turmoil in the banking sector has been reflected in the refusal of many equities analysts to estimate a price for many banks' shares.
"Right now, you would need a crystal ball to estimate bank prices or even financial results for the end of the year," said Tomas Cikrt an analyst at AKRO Capital.
Last week, the central bank freed the crown from its plus/minus 7.5 percent mark/dollar fixing basket after the failure of drastic interest rate hikes to defend the crown.
In order to prevent the crown falling too far, the central bank accompanied the abolition of the bands with a rise in the discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5.
Nevertheless, the crown depreciated by around six percent against the mark and dollar creating potential problems for banks holding foreign currency denominated debt.
"Commercial banks will make losses after the devaluation on their forex exposure," said Henry Woodruff of Atlantik Financni Trhy.
"Foreign currrency debts of banks last year reached the level of about $5.5 billion," he added.
On the other hand, banks which have large volumes of primary deposits are in a position to benefit from the liquidity squeeze on the interbank market.
"Big banks which have a sufficient quantity of primary sources and are not dependent on the interbank market have a large advantage," said AKRO's Cikrt.

Following the crown crisis, the last resort Lombard rate remains at 50 percent - the level it was raised to from 14.9 percent on May 16 to protect the crown - while the one week repo rate was cut to a still high 45 percent from 75 percent on Monday. Overnight interbank rates were 56 percent on Tuesday.

Analysts say that overall, banks face problems from two sides: the risk of non-payment of expensive floating rate loans and possible losses from low interest credits to companies financed from sources demanding high interest rates.
"Banks must count on having more risky loans against which they will have to create reserves or provisions," said Petr Vins of Stratego Invest.
"The impact on bank finances and their profits will therefore be negative...insolvancy among debtors will grow which will mainly affect small banks," he added.

Despite the exceptional reasons for high interest rates, analysts do not anticipate a quick return to pre-crisis rates even if the political situation, which has seen factional fighting within the coalition government, stabilises.

"The main aim of monetary policy will be above all to stem the influence of a depreciated crown on the domestic price level. This aim will entail above all a higher interest rate level on both the deposit and the loan side," said Vins.
